title: Why I chose classification instead of regression for Bitcoin prediction.
author: Public_Luck_4753
selftext:
​

When building a machine learning model for Bitcoin, one of the first decisions is choosing what exactly you want the model to predict. 

Many approaches attempt to predict the future price. 

I decided to approach the problem differently. 

Rather than predicting an exact BTC price, I wanted my model to estimate the probability of a bullish or bearish outcome over a defined five-day period. 

**My reasoning:**

• Exact price prediction introduces another layer of uncertainty.

• Directional classification gives a more practical trading-oriented output.

• Probabilities provide more information than a simple buy/sell label.

• The output can be evaluated against actual subsequent market movements. 

Of course, classification has its own problems, including class imbalance, probability calibration and changing market conditions.

 

I'm curious about how other people approach this.

comments.author: Visible_Let_7292
comments.body: Real challenge is making sure the model is not just learning patterns from past data that disappears when market conditions change.  probably most of these models struggle here .

comments.author: AoideusWasBanned
comments.body: With a 5-day BTC label, adjacent samples share most of the same forward window, so a random split can leak near-duplicate outcomes across train and test. Purge at least five days around the split, fit calibration and any decision threshold on validation only, then compare Brier score and after-fee returns against a simple 5-day momentum baseline, not accuracy alone.

comments.author: Fun-Combination-Arna
comments.body:
I would use binary classification as well, but the choice of model is important.

You may want to consider something more elaborate than simple logistic regression (which provides odds), for instance, an ensemble of different models.

Depending on the nature of your data, if it includes visual data, I would encourage you to explore convolutional neural networks. Finally, based on my experience, you might also be interested in exploring reinforcement learning.

But I wouldn't use a single model unless your classification performs really well with, for instance, something based on naïve k-means or even DBSCAN.

Besides, for rule-based models, you should explore tree-based models and, of course, don't forget gradient-boosting models.

While you might want to start with simple correlation analysis, PCA, or ANOVA to identify relevant features, keep in mind that financial data is not normally distributed and is not stationary. This will restrict which models are suitable or how you should transform and standardize your data first.

Now, you may achieve 80% prediction accuracy, but that doesn't mean you've found a tradable edge, so don't rush. Check always precision and recall, you may have a 90% of accuracy because you only classify correctly what you do not want, because your class of interest is almost missing (sampling is essential).

Finally, take a look at StrategyQuant. You might be pleasantly surprised.

Now, as a side note, price can also be treated as a binary/discrete variable if you associate it with a specific event rather than a continuous price segment.

comments.author: Fluid_Expression_247
comments.body:
Before worrying about classification versus regression, I'm more curious about what gives your model a predictive edge in the first place.
Have you discovered some unique signals or relationships that others have overlooked? If so, congratulations. You might genuinely be onto something.
But if you're relying on patterns in historical prices, volume, and common indicators, how do you know those relationships will hold when market conditions change?
The real question isn't whether your model can predict Bitcoin's direction on historical data. It's whether it can consistently outperform a simple baseline on data it has never seen.

replies.author: Public_Luck_4753
replies.body:
Yes the ML architecture I prepared/modeled is consistently generating positive ROI in live testing also. I have been using it for a whole year now and it still generated ALPHA. And the main thing is, I did not even tweaked the parameters or changed the architure for a single time. 

The model is developed in such a way so that it retrains on newer data every week and this methodology keeps the system adaptive over ever changing market conditions.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Classification makes sense, especially if the probability is what you act on. The main thing I'd watch is overlapping five-day windows: neighbouring samples share most of the same days, so a random train/test split leaks information and makes the result look better than it is. I'd split by time with a gap between train and test, and compare the model against a plain baseline like always guessing the more common outcome. Checking calibration, meaning that 60% calls really come true about 60% of the time, matters just as much as accuracy. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and can hold out the last part of the history, which gives another place to check results.
